## By the end of today

You will have run a complete statistical analysis in R:

::: incremental
- read real data and looked at it
- compared two groups and tested the difference
- visualize and assess patterns in your data
- fit a regression and read the output
:::

::: fragment
It takes twenty-three functions. That is the whole list.
:::

## What today's workshop is not

::: incremental
- a crash course in R programming (e.g., objects, functions, loops)
- a crash course in hypothesis testing

:::

## Today's question

> **Did states that expanded Medicaid in 2014 have lower working-age
> mortality than states that did not?**

## Today's Ballgame

::: incremental
**Explore**: What does mortality look like across states that expanded medicade and those that did not?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ `hist()`, `boxplot()`, group means

**Test**: Is the difference in these states bigger than chance would produce?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ `t.test(rate ~ expanded)`

**Check**: does the answer to our second question depend on unreasonable assumptions?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ permutation test

**Extend**: how can we formally express and model these differences?.
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ `lm(rate ~ expanded)`
:::

## How today works

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Module 1** | I do | I drive. You type every line with me. |
| **Module 2** | We do | Pairs. Most of the code is given; you write the four that matter. |
| **Module 3** | You do | On your own. Eight steps, no code. |

The analysis is the *same shape* all three times. That is deliberate, because by
the third pass, the shape is yours.

## Two rules

::: incremental
1. **Type it, don't read it.** Watching me will not put it in your hands.
   - When you see a code block like this, type it into your script:

     ```{r}
     # a comment: R skips this whole line
     2 + 2   # and everything after a # on a line
     ```
   - What prints underneath (`[1] 4`) is R's answer. Don't type that.
   - `#` starts a **comment**. Your scripts are full of
     them: they are the instructions. Write your code on the blank line
     below, never after a `#`, or R will skip it.
2. **Errors are the job, not a failure.** I will make several on purpose.
   You will make more by accident. This never stops, for anyone.
:::

::: fragment
Red sticky = stuck. Green = through. Put the red one up early.
:::

##

### Module 1: I do

## Two things to name first

Everything in R is an **object** or a **function**.

::: incremental
- An **object** is something you made and gave a name to. It sits in the
  Variables pane until you overwrite it or close R.
- A **function** does something. You give it a name, a pair of parentheses,
  and whatever it needs to know inside them.
:::

::: fragment
That is the whole vocabulary. Every line today is one or both.
:::

## Anatomy of a function call

::: {.anatomy .big}
[read.csv]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=1}[(]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=2}[\"data/medicaid.csv\"]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=3}[,&nbsp;]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=5}[row.names&nbsp;=&nbsp;1]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=4}[)]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=2}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**`read.csv`** is the function name. It says what you want done.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**`( )`** holds everything the function needs to know.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**`"data/medicaid.csv"`** is the first argument: which file to read.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
**`row.names = 1`** is a named argument. It changes how the function
behaves: treat column 1 as row labels, not data. That is why we get 13
columns from a 14-column file.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5}
**`,`** separates one argument from the next.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=6}
Two questions get you through any function: **what do I want R to do**,
and **what does R need to know to do it?**
:::

## Inside the quotes: a path

::: {.anatomy .big}
[\"]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=1}[data/]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=2}[medicaid[.csv]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=4}]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=3}[\"]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=1}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**`" "`** make it a **string**: text, taken as-is. Without them, R reads
`medicaid.csv` as the name of an object, goes looking, and fails.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**`data/`** is a folder. Folder, slash, file: that is a **path**,
directions to the file, starting from the folder you opened.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**`medicaid.csv`** is the file itself.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
**`.csv`** is the **extension**: what kind of file it is. Comma-separated
values, a table saved as plain text. `read.csv()` reads this kind; an Excel
`.xlsx` needs a different function. Finder and File Explorer hide
extensions by default, so you may only see `medicaid` there.
:::

## Mac vs. Windows

The full path to the same file, on two laptops:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Mac** | `/Users/you/01-RStats/data/medicaid.csv` |
| **Windows** | `C:\Users\you\01-RStats\data\medicaid.csv` |

::: incremental
- Ours skips all of that. `data/medicaid.csv` starts from the folder you
  opened, so it is the same on every laptop.
- In R, always write `/`, even on Windows. R reads a lone `\` as the start
  of a special character, so `"data\medicaid.csv"` is an error.
:::

## Step 1: read the data

```{r}
counties <- read.csv("data/medicaid.csv", row.names = 1)
```

Nothing printed. That is what success looks like: `<-` stores silently.

::: fragment
Look at the **Variables** pane. `counties` is now in it.
:::

## Step 1: three questions

```{r}
dim(counties)
```

```{r}
names(counties)
```

```{r}
head(counties, 3)
```

Ask these of every new dataset: **how big, what columns, what's a row.**

## Step 2: look at the outcome

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
hist(counties$crude_rate_20_64)
```

Never test a variable you have not looked at. Defaults are fine; we are not
decorating anything yet.

## What is that `$`?

::: {.codeline style="font-size: 1.3rem;"}
`hist(counties`[`$`]{.pop}`crude_rate_20_64)`
:::

You have not seen that symbol before. **Don't look it up yet.**

::: fragment
Use what is already on the screen:
:::

::: incremental
- `counties` is the table you just read in
- `crude_rate_20_64` was in the list `names()` printed
- so `$` has to join **a table** to **one of its columns**
:::

::: fragment
> "`counties` … the `crude_rate_20_64` one."
:::

## Use the context clues

You just read a symbol you had never seen, correctly, without looking it up.

::: incremental
- Unfamiliar R code is usually surrounded by things you do recognise: a
  table you made, a column you have seen, a function whose name says what
  it does.
- Read around the gap first. The shape of the line tells you what the
  missing piece has to be.
- Then check. Guessing and confirming is faster than looking up cold, and
  you remember it longer.
:::

## Reading from the inside out

`hist(counties$crude_rate_20_64)` has two steps, and the inner one happens
first.

::: incremental
1. `counties$crude_rate_20_64` pulls the column out. On its own it is a
   vector: one number per county.
2. `hist()` draws that vector.
:::

::: fragment
> "Take the `crude_rate_20_64` column out of `counties`, and draw a
> histogram of it."
:::

## Step 3: expansion is a state policy

Every county in Alabama has the same Medicaid policy as every other county
in Alabama.

::: fragment
So the thing that varies is the **state**, not the county. Thirty-nine
states decided; 2,372 counties did not each decide separately.
:::

::: fragment
We need one row per state before we compare anything. That takes three
moves: keep one year, label each state, then average to the state.
:::

## Step 3a: keep one year

```{r}
d2014 <- counties[counties$year == 2014, ]
dim(d2014)
```

::: fragment
Square brackets take a slice: `df[rows, columns]`. We asked for rows where
`year` is 2014, and left the column slot blank to mean "all of them".
:::

::: fragment
`==` asks *is this equal to*. It is a question, not an instruction —
that is why it is doubled.
:::

## Reading a line, right to left

::: {.codeline style="font-size: 1.1rem;"}
`d2014 <- counties[counties$year == 2014, ]`
:::

Longer lines are still one sentence. Start at the right:

::: incremental
- `counties[counties$year == 2014, ]` says *from `counties`, keep the rows
  where `year` is 2014, and every column* …
- `<-` says *… and store it* …
- `d2014` says *… as `d2014`.*
:::

::: fragment
> "**From `counties`, keep the rows where `year` is 2014 and every column,
> and store that as `d2014`.**"
:::

::: fragment
Whatever is left of the arrow is the name you are giving to the result.
If you can say a line out loud, you understand it. If you cannot, that is
where to stop and ask.
:::

## Step 3b: label each state

```{r}
d2014$expanded <- ifelse(!is.na(d2014$yaca) & d2014$yaca == 2014, 1, 0)
table(d2014$expanded)
```

`ifelse(test, value_if_true, value_if_false)` runs down the whole column.

::: fragment
Note `$` doing a second job: on the **left** of `<-` it creates a column
rather than pulling one out.
:::

## Why the `!is.na()` guard

States that never expanded have `yaca = NA`.

::: fragment
`NA == 2014` is not `FALSE`. It is `NA` — R is saying "I don't know."
:::

::: fragment
Without the guard, every one of those rows comes back `NA`, R gives no
error, and every mean you compute afterwards is `NA`. `!` means "not" and
`&` means "and", so the guard reads: *not missing, and equal to 2014.*
:::

::: fragment
Silent wrong answers are worse than errors. This is the most common way R
hands you one.
:::

## Ask R itself

```r
?mean
```

The help page opens in the **Help** pane. The **Usage** line at the top
lists every argument and its default:

```r
mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
```

::: fragment
Three questions for the room:

1. How many arguments does `mean()` take?
2. What does `na.rm` do? (scroll to **Arguments**)
3. What is it set to if you don't say?
:::

## `na.rm = FALSE` is the default

R will not skip missing values unless you tell it to.

```r
mean(counties$median_income)
#> NA
```

Fifteen county-year rows are missing an income. One `NA` is enough to make
the whole answer `NA`.

::: fragment
```r
mean(counties$median_income, na.rm = TRUE)
#> 47.09
```
:::

::: fragment
This is the most common "why is my result `NA`?" in R. When it happens,
`?` the function and look at what its defaults were doing.
:::

## Step 3c: average to the state

```{r}
states_unwt <- aggregate(crude_rate_20_64 ~ state + expanded,
                         data = d2014, FUN = mean)
dim(states_unwt)
```

Read it out loud: *average `crude_rate_20_64`, by state and expansion
status.*

::: fragment
`FUN = mean` passes the function itself, with no parentheses. `FUN = mean()`
would try to run it right now, on nothing.
:::

## The formula: `y ~ x`

That squiggle is the most reusable thing you will learn today.

::: {.codeline style="font-size: 1.5rem;"}
`goal( y ~ x , data = d )`
:::

Read `~` as **"broken down by"**.

| | |
|---|---|
| `aggregate(rate ~ expanded, data = states, FUN = mean)` | group means |
| `boxplot(rate ~ expanded, data = states)` | a picture |
| `t.test(rate ~ expanded, data = states)` | a test |
| `lm(rate ~ expanded, data = states)` | a model |

You have used it once. You will use it four more times before lunch.

## That line hid a decision

```{r}
range(d2014$population_20_64)
```

::: fragment
224 people, and 6.3 million. Averaging county **rates** gave Loving County,
Texas the same weight as Los Angeles.
:::

## A rate is deaths over people

```{r}
d2014$deaths <- d2014$crude_rate_20_64 * d2014$population_20_64 / 1e5

state_deaths <- aggregate(deaths ~ state + expanded, data = d2014, FUN = sum)
state_people <- aggregate(population_20_64 ~ state + expanded, data = d2014, FUN = sum)

states <- state_deaths
states$crude_rate_20_64 <- state_deaths$deaths /
                           state_people$population_20_64 * 1e5

states      <- states[order(states$state), ]
states_unwt <- states_unwt[order(states_unwt$state), ]
```

Add up the deaths, add up the people, divide once. Same `aggregate()`
template, `FUN = sum` instead of `mean`.

::: fragment
Sorting matters: `aggregate()` returns rows grouped, not alphabetically, and
the same `set.seed()` on a different row order gives a different p-value.
:::

## Same 39 states, two different answers

```{r}
gap <- states_unwt$crude_rate_20_64 - states$crude_rate_20_64
summary(gap)

states$state[abs(gap) > 75]
```

::: fragment
Texas is off by more than 130 deaths per 100,000, which is larger than any
difference we are about to look for. We use the weighted version, because
it is the state's actual rate.
:::

## DESCRIBE · Step 4: look at the comparison

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
boxplot(crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded, data = states)
```

```{r}
aggregate(crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded, data = states, FUN = mean)
```

## DESCRIBE · Step 4: the estimate, as one number

```{r}
group_means <- aggregate(crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded,
                         data = states, FUN = mean)
diff_obs <- group_means$crude_rate_20_64[2] - group_means$crude_rate_20_64[1]
diff_obs
```

Expansion states averaged about **64 fewer deaths per 100,000**
working-age people.

Is that more than luck would hand us?

## TEST · Step 5: the test you already know

```{r}
t.test(crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded, data = states)
```

Read all of it. The **interval** tells you the size of the gap the data
supports. The p-value never does.

## Wait, the sign flipped

We computed `diff_obs = −64`. The interval says **+7 to +121**.

::: fragment
That is not an error, and it is not you.

`t.test()` subtracts **group 0 − group 1**. We did **group 1 − group 0**.
Same gap, opposite sign. Check it against the group means at the bottom.
:::

::: fragment
This catches everyone once. When a sign looks wrong, find out which way
round the subtraction went before assuming you broke something.
:::

::: fragment
`t = 2.29` and `df = 34.04` you can ignore today.
:::

## CHECK · Step 6: what does p = 0.13 actually mean?

Most of us walk in carrying this one:

> ~~"p is the probability the result is due to chance."~~

::: fragment
It's the most common answer, and it has the logic **backwards**. A p-value
never tells you the probability that chance caused your result.
:::

::: fragment
It **assumes chance is all there is**, and then asks:

> if expansion made no difference at all, how often would luck alone hand
> us a gap as big as ours?
:::

## CHECK · Step 6: so let's build one

::: incremental
- The null hypothesis says the labels are meaningless.
- So let's *make* them meaningless by shuffling which states expanded.
- Do that a thousand times, and we have a thousand worlds where the policy
  did nothing.
- Then just count how many of them beat our real result.
:::

::: fragment
We don't have to trust a formula for this. **We can just do it.**
:::

## Step 6: one fake world

```{r}
shuffled <- sample(states$expanded)

mean(states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 1]) -
  mean(states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 0])
```

Run it again:

```{r}
shuffled <- sample(states$expanded)
mean(states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 1]) -
  mean(states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 0])
```

That bouncing **is** sampling variation. You are looking straight at it.

## Step 6: a thousand fake worlds

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
diffs <- replicate(1000, {
  shuffled <- sample(states$expanded)
  mean(states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 1]) -
    mean(states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 0])
})
```

`replicate()` does a thing `n` times and keeps the answers.

One thousand worlds in which the policy did nothing.

## Step 6: and there it is

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
hist(diffs)
abline(v = diff_obs, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
mean(abs(diffs) >= abs(diff_obs))
```

Same `hist()` from step 2, pointed at something new. That number is a
p-value you built out of `sample()`, `mean()`, and counting.

## That one line does three things

```r
mean( abs(diffs) >= abs(diff_obs) )
```

| | |
|----|--------------------|
| `abs()` | drops the minus sign, so we count both tails: past −39 and past +39. That is what "two-sided" means, and it is what `t.test()` did. |
| `>=` | gives a `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each of the 1000 shuffles |
| `mean()` | of `TRUE`/`FALSE` gives the proportion that are `TRUE`, because `TRUE` counts as 1 |

## Drop the `abs()` and see

```{r}
mean(diffs >= diff_obs)
```

::: fragment
0.93, not something near 0.07. Our difference is negative, so "shuffles at
least as large as ours" counts almost all of them.
:::

::: fragment
R does not warn you. If you want the one-sided p in the direction of the
effect, it is `mean(diffs <= diff_obs)`. Getting this wrong returns a
number, not an error.
:::

## Why it doesn't exactly match `t.test()`

Permutation gave `0.139`. The t-test gave `0.132`.

::: incremental
- `t.test()` assumes the difference follows a normal distribution. The
  shuffle does not. It does assume the labels could have been dealt out
  any other way, which is true here because each state chose once.
- 1000 shuffles is itself a sample. Change the seed and the second digit
  moves. Run 10,000 if that matters to you.
:::

::: fragment
Two methods, same conclusion: this difference is not distinguishable from
chance with 39 states.
:::

## MODEL · Step 7: the same answer, as a regression

```{r}
m <- lm(crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded, data = states)
summary(m)
```

## MODEL · Step 7: you need two numbers from that

Both on the **`expanded`** row:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `Estimate` | **−39.18** | our difference in means, exactly |
| `Pr(>|t|)` | **0.13** | our p-value |

And one bonus, on the row above: `(Intercept)` is the mean of the group
coded 0 — the same number from step 4. The intercept is just the baseline
group.

::: fragment
Everything else (Residuals, Std. Error, R-squared, F-statistic) answers
questions we haven't asked. You are **not** missing something by skipping
them today.
:::

## MODEL · Step 7: look what happened

A difference in means *is* a regression coefficient.

t-test, permutation test, and regression are three ways of asking one
question, and they agree.

::: fragment
Once you can read this output you can read most quantitative papers.
:::

::: fragment
(`t.test()` uses Welch's correction by default, which is also why its `df` was
34.04 rather than 37. `var.equal = TRUE` matches `lm()` to the decimal.)
:::

## Step 8: why we used 39 rows and not 2,372

```{r}
t.test(crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded, data = d2014)$p.value
```

That is the same test, run on the counties.

::: fragment
`p` is about 6e-17. Overwhelming, and wrong.
:::

::: fragment
It believes it has 2,372 independent observations. It has 39. Every county
in a state shares one policy decision, so those rows repeat 39 pieces of
information rather than adding 2,372 new ones.
:::

::: fragment
When a p-value looks too good, ask how many independent things you actually
measured. It is usually fewer than the number of rows.
:::

## That was the whole game

```
read.csv  dim  names  head  summary     hist  boxplot  abline
ifelse  is.na  table                    aggregate  mean  median  abs  range
c  order                                t.test  lm
sample  set.seed  replicate
```

Twenty-three functions, and you have a difference in means, a permutation test,
and a regression, plus the reason to distrust one of them.

## Glossary: the twenty-three functions

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.58em;"}
**Get data, look at it**

| | |
|---|---|
| `read.csv()` | read a spreadsheet off disk |
| `dim()` | how many rows and columns |
| `names()` | what are the columns called |
| `head()` | show the first few rows |
| `summary()` | six-number sketch of a column |

**Pictures**

| | |
|---|---|
| `hist()` | distribution of one variable |
| `boxplot()` | compare groups |
| `abline()` | add a line to the last plot |

**Build a grouping variable**

| | |
|---|---|
| `ifelse()` | test each value, return 1 or 0 |
| `is.na()` | is this value missing? |
| `table()` | count how many in each category |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.58em;"}
**Summarise**

| | |
|---|---|
| `aggregate()` | apply a function, split by group |
| `mean()` | average, and on TRUE/FALSE a proportion |
| `median()` | the middle value |
| `abs()` | drop the minus sign |
| `range()` | smallest and largest |
| `c()` | glue values into one vector |
| `order()` | the positions that would sort something |

**Test and model**

| | |
|---|---|
| `t.test()` | compare two group means |
| `lm()` | fit a linear model |
| `summary()` | also prints a model's coefficient table |

**The permutation test**

| | |
|---|---|
| `sample()` | shuffle into a random order |
| `set.seed()` | make the shuffling repeatable |
| `replicate()` | do something n times, keep the answers |
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Two more appear only in the finish-early extensions: `plot()` and `sum()`.
:::
:::

::::

## Glossary: the symbols

::: {style="font-size: 0.66em;"}
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `#` | everything after it is ignored | `# this is a note` |
| `<-` | store this as | `x <- 5` |
| `=` | name an argument, *inside* a function | `data = states` |
| `()` | run a function; what it needs goes inside | `mean(x)` |
| `,` | separates one argument from the next | `hist(x, breaks = 20)` |
| `$` | pull one column out of a data frame | `states$expanded` |
| `~` | "broken down by" | `rate ~ expanded` |
| `==` | *is* equal to: a question, not an instruction | `year == 2014` |
| `>=` `<=` `>` `<` | the usual comparisons | `diffs >= 64` |
| `!` | not | `!is.na(x)` |
| `&` | and | `!is.na(x) & x == 2014` |
| `{ }` | treat several lines as one block | inside `replicate()` |
:::

::: fragment
`=` and `<-` both assign, and you will see both. We use `<-` for storing
things and keep `=` for naming arguments. It makes the two jobs visible.
:::

## Glossary: square brackets do three jobs

The one that catches everyone. Same symbol, three different meanings:

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `df[rows, cols]` | slice a **table**, note the comma | `counties[counties$year == 2014, ]` |
| `x[2]` | pick one element out of a **vector** | `group_means$crude_rate_20_64[2]` |
| `x[test]` | keep the elements where a test is TRUE | `states$crude_rate_20_64[shuffled == 1]` |
:::

::: fragment
If you get `undefined columns selected`, you almost certainly left out the
comma in the first form.
:::

## What's new in Module 2

Two things you have not seen:

**Making groups from a number.** Expansion came ready-made as 0/1. Poverty
is continuous, so you split it at the median with `ifelse()`.

**A result that runs off the page.** Your observed difference may fall
outside the whole null distribution:

```r
hist(diffs, xlim = range(c(diffs, diff_obs)))
```

::: fragment
If `mean(abs(diffs) >= abs(diff_obs))` gives you `0`, that is not p = 0.
None of 1000 shuffles got that far, so **report p < 0.001**.
:::

## Two rules for your own work

**Always open the folder.** Never write `setwd("/Users/you/...")`. It works
on exactly one computer, and not for long. Open the project folder and every
path in your script stays relative.

**Never use `rm(list = ls())`.** It does not give you a clean session; it
doesn't unload packages or reset options. Restart R instead:
**Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+0**.

::: fragment
If a script only runs after you have run some *other* thing first, it isn't
finished.
:::

## Common errors to watch for as you start

| You see | What it means, and what to check |
|--------|--------------------|
| `c(1, "two", 3)` gives `"1" "two" "3"` | A vector holds **one type**. One piece of text turns every value into text. Many functions need a specific type, and a mismatch is behind a lot of errors. Check with `class()`. |
| `object 'x' not found` | Nothing by that name exists: a typo (`State` is not `state`), or you skipped the line that makes it. Look in the **Variables** pane. |
| `unexpected symbol`<br>`unexpected ')'` | A typo R can't read, like a missing comma or an extra `)`. R quotes your line up to the point where it got lost. |
| `+` in the Console, not `>` | The line isn't finished. Every `(` needs a `)`: `ifelse(x, ifelse(z == x, 1, 0), NA` opens two and closes one. Type the missing `)`, press Enter, then fix your script. |
| `non-numeric argument to binary operator` | Math (`+ - * /`) on something that isn't a number, like `c(1, "two", 3) + 1`. Check `class()`. |
| `subscript out of bounds` | You asked for a position that isn't there, like `x[[4]]` when `x` has 3 values. Careful: `x[4]` gives no error, just a quiet `NA`. |
